title: HTML Page Structure
subtitle: DOCTYPE, html, head, body — the required bones
author: KERNAL Team

content.text: Every valid HTML document follows a required structure. Whether you're building a personal blog or a web application used by millions, the outer skeleton is always the same.

content.code:
Page Heading

Page content...

content.text: The <!DOCTYPE html> declaration must be the very first thing in any HTML file. It tells the browser this is an HTML5 document. Without it, browsers enter quirks mode — an old compatibility mode that renders pages differently.
Always put <!DOCTYPE html> on the first line. No exceptions. It takes one second and prevents a category of difficult bugs.
The <html> element is the root of the document — everything else is inside it. The lang attribute tells browsers and screen readers the language of the page.

content.code:
<html lang="en">    <!-- English -->
<html lang="hi">    <!-- Hindi -->
<html lang="es">    <!-- Spanish -->
<html lang="ar">    <!-- Arabic (right-to-left) -->

content.text: The lang attribute improves accessibility for screen readers and helps search engines understand the page language. Always include it.
The <head> element contains metadata — information about the page, not content on the page. None of it is visible to the user directly.

items: <meta charset="UTF-8"> — character encoding (always include this; UTF-8 supports every language)
<meta name="viewport"> — controls zoom and layout on mobile devices
<title> — the tab title shown in the browser and in search results
<meta name="description"> — the snippet shown in Google search results
<link rel="stylesheet"> — connects a CSS file to the page
<link rel="icon"> — the favicon shown in the browser tab

content.text: Without the viewport tag, mobile browsers zoom out to show the full desktop layout, making text tiny. This tag is essential for responsive design:
The <body> element contains everything the user sees. Headings, paragraphs, images, forms, buttons — all of it goes inside <body>.
Place <script> tags at the end of the body, just before </body>. This allows the HTML to render before the script runs, making the page feel faster.

questions.question: What does the viewport meta tag do?
options: Sets the font size for the page
Controls how mobile browsers scale the page
Prevents the page from being indexed by search engines
questions.explanation: The viewport meta tag tells mobile browsers not to zoom out to fit the desktop layout. Without it, phones show a tiny, zoomed-out version of the page.

questions.question: Which of these belongs in the <head>, not the <body>?
questions.explanation: <meta> tags go in <head> because they are metadata — information about the page, not visible content. Headings, paragraphs, and images are visible content that belongs in <body>.

questions.question: Placing <script> tags at the end of <body> makes pages load faster.
questions.explanation: Scripts in the <head> block HTML parsing until the script is downloaded and executed. Scripts at the end of <body> allow the HTML to parse and render first, making the page appear faster.

faq.q: What happens if I omit the DOCTYPE?
faq.a: The browser enters 'quirks mode' — a legacy rendering mode that mimics old browsers (IE5, Netscape 4). Your layout will behave inconsistently across browsers. Always include it.
No. A valid HTML document has exactly one <html>, one <head>, and one <body>. Browsers may try to correct extra elements, but the behavior is undefined.

faq.q: Why does the title tag matter for SEO?
faq.a: The <title> is the blue clickable headline in Google search results. It's one of the most important SEO signals. Keep it under 60 characters and make it descriptive.
